title: Building a web API for LangLearner with Spring MVC and Spring Boot
content: Previously, I’ve used the Spring framework with Spring Boot to run a console application. This console application used inversion of control and dependency injection from Spring Core, but was otherwise comparable to my version without Spring. For this next part, I make more extensive use of Spring Boot and Spring MVC in order to construct HTTP endpoints. The end result for this part is a web API, which I can call using a browser or a service such as Bruno.  Revising my Maven structure  Before I construct my API, it’s good to make sure that my web and console versions are properly separated. I’ve left the project structure to IntelliJ thus far, but if I want to make this a multi-module application, I need to take a closer look at it.  First, I’ve separated my existing console application into two modules, called core and console-app. I’ve also created a module called web-services, which will contain my API. Both console-app and web-services import from the core module.  Next, I need to take a look at my Spring dependencies. I could import the dependencies I need individually, but Spring Boot also provides convenient ‘starters’, which are bundles of common Spring dependencies. For my program thus far, IntelliJ has added spring-boot-starter, as well as spring-boot-starter-parent, from which all other starters inherit. I’ll just leave these dependencies in the parent POM file.      <parent>         <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>         <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>         <version>4.0.6</version>         <relativePath/>     </parent>      <dependencies>         <dependency>         <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>         <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>         </dependency>          <!-- Other dependencies -->     </dependencies>   In addition to the dependencies from the parent POM file, my web API also uses spring-boot-starter-web. This starter contains Spring MVC, along with other dependencies which Spring Boot expects to need in a web application.      <dependency>     <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>     <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>     </dependency>   Finally, I need to consider the Spring Boot build in the POM file. If I want Maven to build multiple Spring applications, I need to make sure that the builds for the different main classes are separated. Therefore, I move the Spring Boot build plugin from my original console application to the console submodule.      <plugin>         <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>         <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>         <configuration>             <mainClass>nl.margothteunisse.langlearner.LangLearnerConsole</mainClass>             <layout>JAR</layout>         </configuration>     </plugin>   Likewise, the POM file for my web-services module needs its own build, where I’ve named the the main class LangLearnerApp rather than LangLearnerConsole.  Defining scopes for my components  Having separated the different parts of my application, I can start to build my web API. An important part of that is to consider the scope of the components, which I haven’t discussed thus far.  By default Spring beans are singleton-scoped, which means that Spring creates a single bean when I run the application, and continues to refer to that instance for the whole lifetime of the application. For my console application this was fine, but how would this work in a web application? I can hardly have all users drawing from the same deck!  For these purposes, Spring MVC offers four web-specific scopes. The one that’s relevant for my case is the session scope. A session-scoped bean is initiated whenever a HTTP session is created, and only lasts for as long as the session lasts. I don’t want my vocabulary object to be session-scoped, since it’s a Repository object which might hold a lot of data. It seems preferable to have a single IVocabulary bean, which holds card data which is shared by all users.  By contrast, my Deck component seems like a good contender for being session-scoped. If every HTTP session has its own deck, then I don’t have to worry about users drawing from a shared deck. However, my Deck is a part of my core module, and doesn’t know that it’s being used for a web application. How would I go about making Deck session-scoped, then?  The solution I found comprises two steps. First, I make Deck prototype-scoped. The prototype scope, belonging to Spring Core, entails that a new object reference is created whenever the bean is called upon.  @Component @Scope("prototype") public class Deck {     //Omitted fields      public Deck(IVocabulary vocabulary) {         this.vocabulary = vocabulary;         //Omitted lines     }      //Omitted methods }   In my web-services module, the prototype scoping allows me to define a separate session-scoped Bean, called userDeck, within a configuration class that I’ll call WebConfig. Now, whenever a HTTP session is initiated by a user, Spring will want to instantiate userDeck. Looking for a bean of class Deck, it finds the prototype bean deck, injects it, and creates an instance of it. Based on that specific instance, it creates a session-scoped bean, called userDeck.  @Configuration public class WebConfig {     @Bean     @SessionScope     public Deck userDeck(Deck deck) {         deck.draw();         return deck;     } }    Constructing API endpoints with Spring MVC  With the proper scoping in place, the final step is to construct the API itself. For this, I use the @Controller stereotype from Spring MVC.  When I annotate a class with @Controller, this indicates that the class should listen for HTTP requests. To create a HTTP endpoint, I simply create a method and annotate it with @RequestMapping, or with a more specific annotaiton such as GetMapping.  So what endpoints does my API implement? Based on my Card and Deck objects, I need a user to be able to draw a card. This modifies the deck, so I will annotate this as a POST request. I also need the user to read the current word, which is a GET request. Finally, I need the user to be able to submit an answer, which is also a GET request. I use a request parameter to pass the answer to the API.  For the response, I have my API return JSON data (JavaScript Object Notation) because it makes it easy to check user input. Instead of converting my data to JSON manually, I can make use of another feature of Spring MVC: the @ResponseBody annotation. When I annotate an endpoint with @ResponseBody, Spring MVC knows that it should serialize the output (i.e., convert it to a format that the HTTP protocol understands). The resulting HTTP response body isn’t necessarily in JSON format: for example, if I return a primitive, the HTTP response body will be a primitive as well. Yet, using JSON is a safe bet.  Below I show a mockup of my API, which represents a deck consisting of a single card.  @Controller @RequestMapping("/api") public class WebAPI {     @GetMapping("/drawn-card")     @ResponseBody     public Map<String, String> drawnCard() {         return Map.of("visibleWord", "cat");     }      @GetMapping("/submit")     @ResponseBody     public Map<String, Boolean> submitAnswer(@RequestParam String answer) {        return Map.of("answerIsCorrect", answer == "kissa");     }      @PostMapping("/draw-next-card")     @ResponseBody     public Map<String, Boolean> drawNextCard() {         session.invalidate();         return Map.of("deckIsDepleted", true);     } }    Data transfer objects In my mockup, I use the Map class to return a single piece of JSON information for each of my API calls. Instead of the generic Map offered by Java, I can also use a dedicated object to group my data. I find this approach helpful because it allows me to easily visualize what the frontend should look like, even without writing any HTML. I will tentatively say these objects are based on the common Data Transfer Object (DTO) pattern, and that I can therefore refer to them as such.  I remark that the visibleWord and answerIsCorrect properties together provide a snapshot of the Card class, so I find it natural to group them in an class called CardDTO. In addition, I construct a class called DeckDTO, which contains CardDTO as well as deckIsDepleted. Since CardDTO is included in DeckDTO, I can imagine the resulting web page to look like this:    The actual processing of this information happens on the client side: for the implementation I currently have, I redirect to a different screen with a ‘Play Again’ button when the deck is depleted. The important part for my API, though, is that I can update the part of the page corresponding to CardView without updating DeckView, but not the other way around.  RestController vs Controller  In my API, I’ve used the @Controller annotation. It’s good to note that Spring Boot also offers a @RestController annotation, which adds the @ResponseBody annotation by default. This annotation could save me a few lines of code, yet I purposefully do not use this in my current version.  The reason for that is that the @RestController annotation is intended to be used for APIs following a REST (Representational State Transfer) architecture, and a crucial element of the REST architecture is that it is supposed to be stateless:all the information associated with a particular user’s session should be provided from the client side. Since my API strongly depends on the session-scoped userDeck object, it is decidedly not RESTful.  It’s worth considering what my application would look like with a REST architecture, and I hope to discuss this when I discuss the deployment of my application. For now though, the takeaway is that all RESTful APIs return raw data, but not all APIs which return raw data are RESTful. I therefore want to refrain from using features that are specifically intended for RESTful APIs.   AI DISCLOSURE  Early on, I used Copilot to help make sense of my Spring Boot API. At this point, I had figured out how to make my API listen for HTTP requests, but did not understand what the response should be and how to process it. In particular, I was feeling stuck becuase I did not understand how I could process user input. In brief, I took away the following points from this interaction:  Copilot (using Claude Haiku) immediately recognized that I was lacking static files, and suggested to create an index.html file, along with CSS styling and JavaScript to make a dynamic frontend. I inquired why JavaScript was necessary, and it proceeded to explain the difference between client-side and server-side architectures.   Moreover, since I still had my console application in my project folder, it was able to use this as an example of a server-side application.  At the same time, the LLM also made a mistake in assuming that my API was a REST API. This is not surprising, as I called my web API a REST API in my prompt, and my API was annotated with the RestController annotation. Yet, it did reinforce my own misgiving that a RESTful API was simply a HTTP API which returned JSON data.   Overall, I'm satisfied with my use of Copilot here. At little cost, it helped me to make sense of my application early on, and pointed me towards the right tools. This interaction also showed me how the LLM can build on the information I've provided it with, both in a positive and in a negative sense. On one hand, it was able to better grasp the intention of my project because my project folder ; on the other hand, it also unquestioningly took over my assertion that I had a RESTful API.    Testing my API logic Before, I made a mockup of my API endpoints. For my actual API endpoints, I need to make WebAPI interact with my userDeck object. To access a session-scoped bean from my singleton-scoped API, I can obtain the bean directly from the application context.  @Controller @RequestMapping("/api") public class WebAPI implements ApplicationContextAware {      private ApplicationContext applicationContext;      @Override     public void setApplicationContext(@NonNull ApplicationContext applicationContext)             throws BeansException {         this.applicationContext = applicationContext;     }      @GetMapping("/drawn-card")     @ResponseBody     public CardDTO drawnCard() {         Deck deck = (Deck) applicationContext.getBean("userDeck");          Card card = deck.getDrawnCard();         return new CardDTO(card.read());     }      @GetMapping("/submit")     @ResponseBody     public CardDTO submitAnswer(@RequestParam String answer) {         Deck deck = (Deck) applicationContext.getBean("userDeck");          Card card = deck.getDrawnCard();         boolean answerIsCorrect = card.check(answer);         return new CardDTO(card.read(), answerIsCorrect);      }      @PostMapping("/draw-next-card")     @ResponseBody     public DeckDTO drawNextCard(HttpSession session) {         Deck deck = (Deck) applicationContext.getBean("userDeck");          boolean deckIsDepleted = !deck.draw();         if (deckIsDepleted) {             session.invalidate();         }          return new DeckDTO(deck.getDrawnCard().read(), deckIsDepleted);     } }  The actual API is harder to read than my mockup; it would be good to implement tests to ensure that it keeps working the way I think it does.  When I wrote unit tests for my domain logic, I used JUnit, but that’s not sufficient in this case. After all, my API takes the userDeck object from a Spring application context; how am I going to test that? For this purpose, Spring offers a test context, which is a part of the Spring Boot test starter.  Since I’ve already tested my Deck object, I’m using Mockito to mock the userDeck object. Spring Boot offers the @MockitoBean annotation to mock a Deck object and add it as a bean in my test context. I’m also using MockHttpSession to check if the HTTP session is invalidated when the deck is depleted.  It’s good to note that my userDeck mock is a singleton, unlike the real userDeck from WebConfig which is session-scoped. This works well for testing WebAPI in isolation: I can load the application context once, and set my userDeck outputs as I please. That said, I might want to add a more involved test at a later point to make sure that my session-scoped deck is functioning the way I expect it to.  Running and accessing my API Now that I’ve constructed my API, all I need to do is to let Spring Boot put all my components together in an application:  @SpringBootApplication public class LangLearnerApp {      public static void main(String[] args){         SpringApplication.run(LangLearnerApp.class);     } }    When I run the application, Spring Boot recognizes that I’m using spring-boot-starter-web, and consequently runs its embedded TomCat server on port 8080. Once I have started the application, I can use a service like Bruno to consume the API endpoints.  First, I will read the drawn card:    Next, I submit my answer, which can be correct or incorrect:    I can draw a new card:    Finally, if the deck is depleted upon drawing, it communicates this information and resets:    Having ensured that my endpoints behave as I expect them to, I can start to build my frontend.  The described version of my LangLearner application can be found here.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.

title: Converting my Language Learning App to Spring Boot
content: This is the second part in a series where I build a language learning app using Java and Spring Boot. Please see this post for an overview of the project.  In the previous part of my LangLearner project, I constructed a console application in Java using domain-driven and test-driven design. In this part, I want to take some time to delve into the Spring framework and Spring Boot, and how it can help to make my application more robust.  Why use a framework?  As I understand it, frameworks encompass the ‘plumbing’ of an app: technical concerns such as handling HTTP requests, connecting to a database, security, or logging, which do not depend on the domain logic. Frameworks are widely employed in modern software engineering for a few reasons:     Frameworks save the developer the time and effort of building their own code structure.   Frameworks are less susceptible to bugs than custom code.   Because frameworks are widely adopted, they provide a common language between developers.   I won’t get into these reasons in detail; for that, I’m happy to refer to the wonderful Spring Start Here1. The better question for me at this time is: why do I want to use Spring for my project? That informs what aspects of the Spring framework I should look to.  In my case, there are two things I want to do with Spring:     Handing over initialization to Spring by using the Spring Core application context   Creating an API using Spring MVC   In this post, I will focus on the first part. The end product for this part will be a Spring Boot console application.  Adding Beans to Spring’s application context  To understand how Spring works, it helps to note that my ‘main function’ actually has two separate responsibilities. First, it instantiates the application, by creating a Deck connected to a Vocabulary. Second, it runs the application exactly once.  To make this separation more explicit, I can extract the functionality for running the application to a separate class, which I’ll call ConsoleSession.  public class ConsoleSession {     private final Deck deck;      public ConsoleSession(Deck deck) {         this.deck = deck;     }      public void run() {         //Draw cards until deck is exhausted.     } }   My LangLearnerConsole class now looks like this:  public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         ConsoleSession session = new ConsoleSession(Deck(Vocabulary("wordlist.txt")));         session.run();     } }   In the first line of my main function I instantiate my application, and in the second line I run it. Spring can augment both steps but for now, I will focus on the initialization step.  A foundational concept in the Spring framework is Inversion of Control (IoC). Inversion of control means that, instead of instantiating and connecting objects myself, I hand fine-grained control of select objects (called Beans) over to Spring. The basic structure of my main function then looks like this:  public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(LangLearnerConsole.class);         context.getBean(ConsoleSession.class).run();     } }   Note that, in this new version, I’m not specifying any details about the application in the initialization step. This is by design: it prevents me from putting doman logic in the application’s main method. Instead, I tell Spring to initialize its application context.  Currently the application context is empty, so the application can’t run yet. If I request a Bean of type ConsoleSession, Spring will return an error. To make the application run, I need to make Spring aware of the required Beans.  There are multiple ways to add Beans to Spring’s application context, but an oft-preferred method is to use stereotype annotations. Stereotype annotations are added above class definitions, and tell Spring to create exactly one instance of that class. For example, I can add an instance of ConsoleSession to Spring’s application context by annotating it with @Component2.  @Component public class ConsoleSession {     private final Deck deck;      public ConsoleSession(Deck deck) {         this.deck = deck;     }      //Omitted ConsoleSession methods }   For Spring to instantiate a console session, it will also need a Deck. Again, I tell Spring to instantiate a Deck by annotating it with @Component.  @Component public class Deck{     private final IVocabulary vocabulary;     private Card drawnCard;      Deck(IVocabulary vocabulary) {         this.vocabulary = vocabulary;     }      //Omitted Deck methods }   I don’t need to annotate Card as a component, since I’m not using any of Spring’s functionalities for these. However, I am going to need an IVocabulary object in order to instantiate my Deck. To do that, I place a stereotype annotation above the TextVocabulary class. The interface itself is never annotated, since interfaces hold no meaning to Spring.  I annotate TextVocabulary with @Repository. This stereotype inherits from @Component, and therefore tells Spring to create exactly one instance of the class. However, using @Repository is preferable here because it also provides information about the role of TextVocabulary, both to Spring and to anyone reading the code.  @Repository public TextVocabulary implements IVocabulary {     //Omitted fields     public TextVocabulary(String filename) {        //Omitted file reading     }     //Omitted IVocabulary implementations }   Finally, I need to provide Spring with a filename for TextVocabulary to read out. I can’t use a stereotype annotation for this, since that would require me to directly modify the String class. Instead, I can manually create a @Bean of type String within my LangLearnerConsole class. I annotate LangLearnerConsole as a @Configuration to indicate that it can be a source of Beans. I also annotate it as @ComponentScan to make it look for stereotype annotations.  @Configuration @ComponentScan public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String [] args) {         var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(LangLearnerConsole.class);         context.getBean(ConsoleSession.class).run();     }      @Bean     public String filename() {         return "wordlist.txt";     } }   Now, Spring has enough information to construct its application context: it uses the filename I provided to instantiate a TextVocabulary, which it uses to instantiate a Deck, which in turn is used to instantiate a ConsoleSession. Note that I never explicitly specified how these objects should be connected; because the structure is so simple, Spring can ‘auto-wire’ the objects. For a more complex app this process, called dependency injection (DI), is more involved.  My console application runs now, but as a downside, the name of my vocabulary file is now hard-coded in this @Bean method. For the final part of this post, I will externalize my vocabulary file name by using Spring Boot and its application.properties file.  Externalizing my vocabulary file with Spring Boot  Spring Boot is a part of the Spring ecosystem, of which the core idea is ‘convention over configuration’. Spring itself offers extensive configuration options, but for many use cases, such customization is not necessary. Spring Boot provides many preconfigured functionalities which make it easier to set up a Spring application.  I will use two features offered by Spring Boot for my console application. Most importantly, I will use Spring Boot’s application.properties file to store my vocabulary file. I will also use Spring Boot’s CommandLineRunner interface to make my LangLearnerConsole class a little more concise.  In Spring Boot, application.properties is a standard file used for configuration. When I store the name of my vocabulary file in application.properties, I can directly access it in TextVocabulary:  vocabulary.filename: wordlist.txt   @Repository public TextVocabulary implements IVocabulary {     //Omitted fields     public TextVocabulary(@Value("${vocabulary.filename}") String filename) {        //Omitted file reading     }     //Omitted IVocabulary implementations }   To make use of application.properties and other Spring Boot features, I need to call the SpringApplication.run method, and add the @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation. Since the combination of @Configuration, @Componentscan and @EnableAutoConfiguration is used so often, Spring Boot lets me replace all of them by @SpringBootApplication.  In addition to using application.properties, I’ve also marked my ConsoleSession class as a CommandLineRunner. This is an interface provided by Spring Boot, which signals that arun method (with potential program arguments) should automatically be run when the CommandLineRunner is part of a Spring Boot application. That exactly fits the function which my ConsoleSession fulfills.  Thanks to these Spring Boot features, my LangLearnerConsole class now requires minimal information about the underlying application.  @SpringBootApplication public class LangLearnerConsole {      public static void main(String[] args) {         SpringApplication.run(LangLearnerConsole.class).close();     }  }   With this, I’ve successfully converted my console application to a Spring Boot application. The console output is the same as in the previous part, in essence, but it’s now surrounded by information provided by Spring Boot’s autoconfiguration. I can tell that the application is a Spring Boot application by its header:    .   ____          _            __ _ _  /\\ / ___'_ __ _ _(_)_ __  __ _ \ \ \ \ ( ( )\___ | '_ | '_| | '_ \/ _` | \ \ \ \  \\/  ___)| |_)| | | | | || (_| |  ) ) ) )   '  |____| .__|_| |_|_| |_\__, | / / / /  =========|_|==============|___/=/_/_/_/   :: Spring Boot ::                (v4.0.6)   The next step is to go from my current console application to a web API. Spring Boot is especially useful for this, as I show in the next part.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.                 Laurenţiu Spilcă. Spring Start Here (2021). ↩︎                 In my actual code I use Controller rather than Component, but I prefer to get into this when I discuss my RESTful API in the next part. ↩︎

title: A Console App for Language Learning with Domain-Driven and Test-Driven Design
content: This is the first part in a series where I build a language learning app using Java and Spring Boot. Please see this post for an overview of the project.  In this first part of my LangLearner project, I will work out the design of my application. As already mentioned in the overview, I will be using test-driven design for this. In addition, I will use UML diagrams, specifically class and sequence diagrams, to visualize my design. The end product for this part is a console application in Java.  Building the domain model  The first step in building my language learning application is to ask what my domain logic is. In other words: how will my app help someone to learn vocabulary? A good way to figure this out is to pay close attention to the nouns and verbs that people are naturally inclined to use 1.  Traditionally, if I want to learn a language I might use a deck of flash cards. Whenever I draw a card, I read the front of the card, and try to translate the word. I then check whether my translation matches the back of the card, before moving on to the next card.  So I will need a Deck, which allows me to draw a Card from it. A Card has a front and a back. I need to be able to read the front, and check that my answer matches the back. I might want to add more functionalities, like shuffling the deck, or showing the correct answer to the user, but I think this is a good minimal model to start with.  To describe my Deck and Card objects I can draw a UML class diagram which looks something like this:    As you can see, my class diagram is closely tied to my description above. The only refinement I’ve made is that I’ve added a getter method, getDrawnCard. This method exists to avoid draw from taking on multiple responsibilities (modifying the deck, and returning a Card object).  There’s still one glaring issue that I’m left with here, though: where is the Deck coming from? The way it looks now, it seems as though I need to manually provide the cards property to the Deck. That might work for a few words, but it’s clearly not very convenient for a language learning app! I’ll get back to that, but before that, I will first implement these functions.  Implementing scenarios with test-driven design  As noted in my overview, I am applying test-driven design, which means I’m writing the tests for my classes and methods before I write their implementations. To know what tests I should write, I can consider the different scenarios which may occur:     The user draws a card and translates it correctly.   The user draws a card and translates it incorrectly.   There are no more cards remaining in the deck.   I can work out these three scenarios more fully using sequence diagrams. I’ll start with the scenario where there are no more cards remaining in the deck, since that is the simplest case. All I need to do is tell the user that they’re done.    Now for the scenario where the user successfully draws a card. I don’t think I need to distinguish between the cases where the user translates correctly or incorrectly, as the only difference between the two right now is in the feedback that the user receives. I end up with this sequence diagram:    Based on these sequence diagrams, I’ve written my tests and worked out my domain model. Again, I’m still creating my Deck manually, but for testing purposes this is not a problem.  The Repository pattern  I mentioned that it was not quite clear where the Deck was coming from. Now it’s time to address this point. For my original LangLearner program, I would simply have the program read out my vocabulary from two columns in a .txt file. I could do the same in my current model, by providing my Deck with a .txt file to read out.  However, I would prefer not to put the logic for reading out a file in the constructor of Deck. This would hide too much complexity in my Deck object, and muddle my design. It’s better to give the responsibility for reading out and storing vocabulary to a separate domain object, which I’ll call TextVocabulary.    This is already a lot better than what I had before. Now that TextVocabulary is responsible for reading out and storing vocabulary, I can keep Deck simple.  At the same time, I now have the issue that my Deck depends on TextVocabulary. This is a problem because TextVocabulary is not a part of my domain logic. As the app develops, I might want to store my vocabulary data in a different format like SQL or NoSQL (e.g., MongoDB). I don’t want to overhaul my entire design when I reach that point.  That’s where we get to the widely-used Repository pattern. The idea of the Repository pattern is that, no matter what is happening under the hood, it behaves as though all data were directly stored in memory 12. To achieve this, I can create an interface, which I call IVocabulary.    Thanks to this IVocabulary interface, it’s now clear where the boundary of my domain model lies: IVocabulary is a part of the domain, but its implementations, including TextVocabulary, are not.  Now, I want to emphasize that using a text file for the vocabulary is not necessarily a problem, especially for language learning! When I come across a new word while reading or listening, I don’t want to have to stop what I’m doing to put these words in a database. I just want to jot the word down and move on. That’s why, to this day, I still use those same text files to keep track of my vocabulary.  So it doesn’t have to be a bad thing that my ‘database’ just reads out a text file. It only becomes an issue when I’m tied down to it.  Building a console application  The first version of my app is almost complete now. I can create a Deck from a Vocabulary, draw Cards from the deck, read the words on the front of the cards, and check whether a given translation is correct. All that I need to do now is to put it all together. I could create a class with a main function which loops over the cards:   public class LangLearnerConsole {     public static void main(String @NonNull [] args) {         try  {             Deck deck = new Deck(new TextVocabulary(args[0]));              Scanner scn = new Scanner(System.in);             while (deck.draw()) {                 System.out.println("Translate: " + deck.readCard());                 String answer = scn.nextLine();                 if (deck.translateCard(answer)) {                     System.out.println("Correct!");                 }                 else {                     System.out.println("That is incorrect.");                 }             }             System.out.println("You have translated all words!");         } catch (IOException e) {             System.out.println("Could not find file.");         }     } }    This produces a working Java application, though a very simple one. As an example, I have an input called wordlist.txt, which contains two comma-separated columns of words, in English and Finnish respectively.  cat, kissa dog, koira bird, lintu bear, karhu  If I provide this file as an argument for my Java app, then it draws these cards in order, allows me to submit a translation, and gives me feedback:    As you can see, the application works as intended. Still, it’s not very satisfying. Even though I carefully constructed my domain model, I still have this vague ‘main function’ to worry about. So how can I improve on this process? Well, that’s where a framework like Spring comes in. I will discuss this in the next post.  The console app described in this post can be found here.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.  References  UML diagrams made using Excalidraw.                Eric Evans. Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. ↩︎ ↩︎2                 Harry Percival & Bob Gregory. Architecture patterns with Python. ↩︎

title: Building a Language Learning App with Java and Spring Boot
content: When I was just starting to learn Python, I got the idea to use it to build a language learning application. The idea was simple: pick a word from a vocabulary list, ask the user to provide the translated word, and have the program check if the user is correct. To test the application, I used a short list of Finnish words, as I had had an interest in learning the language.  As it turns out, I would extensively use this program in my language learning journey. What I liked about it was that I could use my personal vocabulary list, and I didn’t need to put in any extra effort. Whenever I updated my vocabulary list with a new word, I could immediately use that. I also experimented with other features. The most important of these was a save function, as my vocabulary grew from a couple hundred to a couple thousand.  In the years since, I’ve been continuing to learn Finnish, yet my LangLearner application has grown somewhat neglected. That’s where this project comes in.  Overview  A web showcase of my application is now live! It is available via Render at: langlearnerapp.onrender.com     A Console App for Language Learning with Domain-Driven and Test-Driven Design   Converting my Language Learning App to Spring Boot   Building a web API for LangLearner with Spring MVC and Spring Boot   Goals My goal for this project is  to rebuild my LangLearner application from scratch, while sticking true to the spirit of the original program. While I originally used Python, for this new version I’ve chosen to use Java. It’s a language that I’ve been wanting to use more, and I think it is more natively suited for building applications than Python.  I’ve also been wanting to dip my toes into the Spring framework. I think LangLearner will be well-suited for that, as the appliciation itself is relatively simple, but at the same time it requires both a database and a user interface.  My goals are therefore as follows:     Build a domain in Java to pull pairs of words (‘flash cards’) from a deck, and check these against user input.   Have this domain comply with the Spring framework.   Build a database which can store custom vocabulary lists based on .txt files.   Implement a save/load function to deal with long vocabulary lists.   Build a simple user interface.   Methods  For this project I’m following domain-driven design (DDD), which is an approach where a domain model is at the center of the software. To ensure that my domain model is robust, I’m also applying test-driven design (TDD): writing failing tests first, and writing implementation to make the tests pass.  I’m writing my application in Java, as its object-oriented nature synergizes well with domain-driven design. I’m also using IntelliJ IDEA to write and execute my code.  Finally, in the spirit of agile development, I want to divide this project into manageable chunks, where I have a viable application at the end of each one. Even as a solo developer, that helps my sanity, and it has the added bonus of keeping these blog posts at a manageable level.  The code for my project is available on my Github. As a disclaimer, I will say that at the point of writing, I’ve already completed the first three parts of the project: constructing a console application, converting this application to Spring Boot, and using Spring Boot to construct a web API. Therefore, my version history on GitHub might deviate from the order in which I’ve written these posts.  Except where explicitly specified, generative AI was not used for this project.
